paper_title: Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within $10^{-4}$ bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.

sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: Models. We train latent feedback Transformers of 135M and 780M parameters with = 3 MTP heads. The baseline is standard Transformer with the same backbone and heads but without feedback. Appendix describes the architecture and training. Training and data. Each run trains for one epoch on prefix of the Dolma 3 mix [10], 13.4B tokens for 135M and 77.8B tokens for 780M. Every setting uses the learning rate and weight decay tuned for the standard Transformer, and trains with three seeds. Evaluation. We evaluate quality on seven subsets of Paloma [11] and average the BPB over these subsets. We measure speed as the steady-state throughput of batched engine that serves the first turns of the Spec-Bench and SPEED-Bench prompts [12, 13] with continuous batching, relative to exact decoding in the same engine at the same batch size. For downstream quality, we measure the BPB of the gold answers in the Olmo 3 Base Easy suites [10]. All models decode greedily in float16. We report batch size 1 in Section 4.2 and other batch sizes in Section 4.3. We compare exact decoding with verifying = 3 drafts under pipelined correction with = 0 to 3 corrections. Unless noted, we report means over three seeds, with standard deviations as terms or error bars. Appendix describes the full protocol.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation study
sections.content: Stand-ins. We first ask why state alignment is the right stand-in. Within one call, the stand-ins trade one-call error against ceiling drop  (Table 2)  . On one hand, zeros and the MTP state as stand-ins keep the ceiling but have several times the one-call error of state alignment.1 On the other hand, in-place substitution has the lowest one-call error but lowers the ceiling. State alignment avoids both problems. Its loss trains only the map and leaves the backbone untouched, so it keeps the ceiling with small one-call error and extra compute. With one correction, it serves the feedback ceiling nearly as fast as in-place substitution and at lower BPB (Figure 5). On downstream tasks, state alignment also keeps most of feedbacks advantage (Appendix D). Number of corrections. We next look for the number of corrections that balances quality and speed. Without correction (D = 0), the approximation error is still nonnegligible. Fortunately, one pipelined correction (D = 1) removes almost all of it while keeping most of the speedup (Figure 5). This correction is inexpensive since it runs in the same call that verifies the next drafts, so each round needs one call instead of D+1 (Figure 4). This speeds up the decoding considerably. However, it still lags behind standard speculative decoding for two reasons  (Table 3)  , which together trade speed for quality: More positions in single call. Each call verifies the new drafts and the positions that still need correction. At small batch sizes, these positions are cheap, but they take time once each call becomes computebound. More accurate verification. When we check each draft against state that reads corrected feedback instead of stand-in, we reject some drafts that one-call verification would accept, which reduces the tokens per call from = 0 to = 1 by 2 to 4% for the trained stand-ins and by 8 to 11% for zeros, which simply drop the feedback at drafted positions. To check whether errors compound once the model generates on its own, we sample free generations of 1,024 tokens at temperature 1 and compare the distribution of each served token with that of exact decoding (Table 4 in Appendix B). With one correction, the KL divergence of state alignment is below 6 4 nats per token, and second correction lowers it about twentyfold more. So, the error remains small 10 even for long generations. Moreover, when greedy decoding departs from exact decoding, it mostly first 1The 780M MTP states error in Table 2 spans wide range because each seeds heads set one coordinate of their state differently. The output head ignores this coordinate, so the MTP loss leaves it free, but the feedback reads it (Appendix C). 6 Figure 5: BPB of the 780M model on each evaluation set against the speedup over exact decoding. Figure 8 in Appendix shows 135M. departs at near-tie, token that exact decoding itself scores within 0.1 nats of its own choice, although near-ties make up under 1% of the positions (Table 5 in Appendix B). So, with one correction, the free generation remains close to exact decoding, which makes = 1 the setting we recommend. Batch size and serving. When batching many requests, the Feedback Shortcut remains faster than exact decoding at each batch size (Figure 6). At small ones, state alignment with one correction decodes 2.36 to 2.75 times faster than exact decoding, close to the Transformers 2.49 to 2.93 times. However, as the batch fills the GPU, each call becomes compute-bound, and the positions that correction verifies start to take time. At batch size 256, = 1 is still about 1.7 times faster than exact decoding, but it lags further behind the Transformer. In this regime, server could switch to one-call verification (D = 0), which decodes about as fast as the Transformer but with better performance, though It keeps only 80 to 85% of feedbacks advantage (Figure 5). This offers heavily loaded services way to trade model quality for serving cost.

sections.title: 5 Related work
sections.content: Feedback Transformers. Feedback Transformers feed the high-level state of each position to later positions and report performance gains [13, 14, 15]. However, this sequential dependence breaks speculative decoding, whose verifier computes all drafted positions in single call while each of them needs the toplayer state of the previous position. Feedback Shortcut is step toward removing this obstacle, allowing these models to be served with speculative decoding. Speculative decoding. Speculative decoding drafts tokens cheaply and verifies them with single forward pass of the target, which preserves the targets output [4, 5, 16]. Drafts come from small models [17], from the targets own layers [18, 19], from block diffusion [20], or from heads on the targets states [2123]. Multi-token prediction (MTP) trains these heads along with the model, in parallel [6] or 7 Figure 6: Speedup over exact decoding against batch size B, excluding prefill and the CPU work between calls. One-call verification (D = 0) is as fast as the Transformer at every batch size, and larger trades speed for accuracy. as chain [7, 24]. NextLat [25] regresses the models next top-layer state as an auxiliary loss that shapes (1) the model and as source of drafts. We instead pull the MTP state toward t+k, the first-pass state that the second pass reads, and train only map, so the stand-in can serve as feedback without changing the model (Section 2). Pipelined inference. If each output needs several sequential steps using same function module, the next output can start before the current one finishes and share its batched call. Looped Transformers pipeline across depth [2630], and video diffusion pipelines across denoising steps [3133]. Our pipelined correction shares similar spirit. Each call corrects the positions that read stand-ins while verifying the next drafts, making the verification more accurate without extra calls.

sections.title: 6 Conclusions
sections.content: Latent feedback breaks speculative decoding because drafted position needs to read state that is still being computed in its verification call. We remove this obstacle by training the stand-in to be read as feedback and by correcting the drafted positions while verifying the next drafts. This recovers most of the speedup that speculative decoding gives Transformer, at quality close to that of the feedback model. Limitations The Feedback Shortcut is still not exact. Closing the remaining gap needs stand-in that adds less error while keeping the ceiling. We leave such stand-in and larger-scale experiments to future work.

sections.title: A Training and evaluation details
sections.content: Models. We use 135M models with 12 blocks of 768 width each and 780M models with 24 blocks of 1536 width each. The backbone is pre-norm decoder with RMSNorm [34], rotary positions [35], QKnorm [36] and SwiGLU [37] with untied embeddings. Feedback is fed into the first block of the decoder using the linear fusion of Eq. 1. One training pass is run with probability 0.31 and two with probability 0.69. For updates with two training passes, the first pass is run without gradient and the losses are computed in the second pass. The MTP heads are trained with loss weight 0.3 throughout training, as in DeepSeek-V4 [38]. Training. For training the matrices, we use NorMuon [39]. For the embeddings and the output head, we use AdamW [40]. We use learning rate that increases during the first 1% of the updates and then decays linearly to zero during the last 20% of the updates [41]. Every setting uses the learning rate and weight decay that perform best for the Transformer on grid of one-epoch runs for each model size. These values are also the best for latent feedback at 780M, and at 135M they are 0.0025 nats per token worse on the validation set than latent feedbacks best. Each update processes 256 sequences of 2,048 tokens. The data is single shuffled stream of the 150B-token Dolma 3 mix, tokenized with the Llama 2 tokenizer [42]. Stand-ins. State alignments map has 3.7M parameters at 135M and 14.9M at 780M, with hidden width 2,048 and 4,096; its RMSNorm has no learned scale. Each training window of in-place substitution extends past each of its positions with probability 0.75. Quality. We score each Paloma document on its own for exact BPB, as Paloma scores documents. We measure the one-call error ϵ1 teacher-forced on windows of the concatenated documents, with all earlier windows being corrected, so that only the current window reads stand-ins. Downstream answers are scored as OLMES scores answers, after the document-start token the models were trained with. Served quality. To measure the quality of what is served by speculative decoding, the decoding loop is run on fixed text. For each call of the loop, tokens are generated with the MTP heads and the pending positions are verified under pipelined correction with corrections. Each committed token is equal to the corresponding token in the fixed text, and draft is kept only while it is equal to the fixed text. Each token is scored by the distribution of its predecessor in the call that committed it. On Paloma, the loop is run on the windows of the one-call error after prefilling each windows first 33 tokens, and Figure 5 adds the difference between served and exact BPB measured there to the exact BPB of the whole documents. For the downstream suites, the context is prefilled and the answer is decoded with the same loop, which measures the served BPB directly. Decoding and timing. All evaluations, including timings, are performed in float16, following SpecBench [12]. The models are trained in bfloat16 mixed precision, but the largest activations are at least 7 smaller than the largest value in float16, and the finer rounding of float16 keeps greedy text closer to float32 decoding than bfloat16 mixed precision. Prefill runs 4 parallel passes of Eq. 2 over the prompt, and exact decoding uses the same prefill. Each answer is decoded to at most 256 new tokens. The singlerequest timings of Appendix synchronize the GPU at the boundaries of each request, include prefill and the CPUs bookkeeping, and count the tokens of both decoders as they are emitted. Batched engine. To obtain the speeds reported in Section 4, we implemented batched engine on single GPU. It takes as input the first turns of Spec-Benchs 480 questions as well as the 435 SPEEDBench prompts not contained in Spec-Bench, which are randomly ordered and cycled into queue of size max(300, 8B) requests. The engine then serves this queue of requests from slots using continuous 11 Algorithm 1 Greedy decoding with Feedback Shortcut. holds the pending positions, is the last position whose state is final, and yj = arg maxv p(v hj). 1: Prefill x1:c and commit xc+1; dc , 2: repeat 3: max(W {c}) ˆxs+1 ys; draft ˆxs+2:s+1+K and as+1:s+K from hs 4: 5: {s+1, . . . , s+1+K} 6: 0 if > s+1, else dj1 + 1, for all dj Compute hj and yj for all in one call 7: 8: while c+1 and dc+1 xc+2 yc+1; c+1 9: and ˆxc+1 = xc+1 do end while 10: 11: {j : > c, ˆxi = yi1 for all < j} 12: until xc+1 is the end token MTP chain Eq. 7 Eq. 3 if dj = 0, else Eq. 6 commit reject batching. Each request is stopped at the end token or after 256 new tokens, and its slot then prefills the next prompt in the queue between calls. Each call then packs the pending positions of all slots, so each request computes only its own pending positions and drafts, and exact decoding is also run in the same engine. Throughput is the number of committed tokens per second, over the calls in which all slots are busy with requests from the queue. Each call is timed from the upload of its rows to the GPU until its summary is returned to the CPU, so prefill and the CPUs bookkeeping between calls are not timed. sections.title: C Drafting Quality Does Not Determine Readability
sections.content: Table 6 compares each heads drafting quality against its single-call error and exact BPB across seeds. Within each model scale, every seed and setting achieves nearly identical drafting quality, yet the error spans over three orders of magnitude. Because the MTP loss constrains an MTP heads hidden state solely through the output head, the remaining dimensions of the state are left unconstrained. State alignment reads these head states via learned projection while keeping their training unchanged; in-place substitution instead exploits this freedom to make the raw state directly readable. Neither approach degrades drafting quality. This unconstrained subspace explains why the 780M MTP states vary sharply across seeds. In every 780M model, single coordinate of the top-layer hidden state carries over half of the total energy after RMSNorm, yet the final norm assigns it near-zero gain, rendering it invisible to the output head. Consequently, the MTP loss leaves this coordinate unconstrained in the head states: Seed 1 happens to match the models true value, Seed 2 flips its sign in Head 1, and Seed 0 leaves it near zero in Heads 1 and 2 while concentrating energy on different coordinate. However, the feedback path reads RMSNorm(a) without the final norms gain, turning any mismatch at this coordinate into large error for the reader. To verify this causally, we clamp this coordinate and the stand-ins largest coordinate to their empirical means from the models states. The cross-seed error spread drops from roughly 40-fold to 2-fold, though all seeds still incur higher error than zero-vector baseline. 14 Table 6: Each seeds drafting quality beside its one-call error ϵ1 and exact decoding BPB on Paloma. heads acceptance is one minus the total variation between its draft and the exact next-token distribution, teacher-forced, and head is scored only where heads 1 to 1 were accepted. sections.title: D Uncertainty of Downstream Differences
sections.content: Downstream BPB varies across both training seeds and benchmark items; HumanEval, for instance, contains only 164 problems. Because item-level noise shifts all models similarly and largely cancels out in paired comparisons on identical items, the error bars in Figure 7 reflect seed variance only. Table 7 reports pairwise differences incorporating both uncertainty sources. The seed variance follows Welchs t-test across each models three seed scores. The item variance is estimated via paired bootstrap as the standard error of the mean difference over 2,000 item-level resamples, using identical resampled item sets across both models and all seeds. The two components are summed in variance, with effective degrees of freedom computed via the WelchSatterthwaite approximation.
